klo: Critically examine how functional expertise, personality, cognitive bias and emotional conditions influence the interpretation of strategy.
Demonstrate shared strategic understanding and commitment across the leadership system.
Recognise the organisational conditions that strengthen or weaken strategic alignment.
Formulate a coherent enterprise interpretation that supports consistent decisions and coordinated action.

sections.label: Facilitator Guide
sections.sub: Use this tab to prepare before each section. It contains the unit intent, key facilitation questions, and tone and watch points for the full unit.

guidance: ◆ Unit Intent

Unit 5 establishes the human operating system of execution. Strategy moves through people, and functional expertise, bias and emotion shape how each leader interprets it. The unit builds a shared enterprise interpretation and the behaviours that sustain commitment.
SCARF explains resistance, ACE-IT sets the behaviour standard and COMPASS locates the hot zones. The Section 5 exercise, in which leaders map how their roles connect, is the centrepiece.
◆ Key Facilitation Questions
“What is the dominant emotion your team carries into the current strategy, and how does it change what people invest?”
“Which SCARF trigger does the current strategy activate most for your people?”
“Which COMPASS zone would flare first in your organisation under pressure? What is the early warning?”
“What behavioural change will you model in the next month so others can see alignment in action?”
◆ Tone & Watch Points
Watch for: compliance mistaken for commitment. Probe: “Would they still act this way if no one were checking?”
Watch for: emotion treated as a side topic. Connect each emotional state to an execution consequence.
Watch for: commitments that describe intentions. Each behavioural change must be observable by the team.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Interrogative Anchor · Before any strategy can be executed, it must travel through people. People arrive at every strategy meeting carrying a personality profile, emotional defaults, and personal motives that determine how much energy they will invest in the organisation’s goals.
slo: Examine how functional expertise, cognitive bias and emotion shape the interpretation of strategy.
Recognise the triggers of resistance and the behaviours that sustain alignment.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1 · Awareness

Section intent: Establish the foundational insight that strategy is first and foremost a human interpretation problem. Leaders must feel this before they can act on it. Resist the urge to move to solutions quickly — create space for recognition.

Opening provocation: “Think of a strategy that was perfectly designed and then failed in execution. What broke? Was it the plan — or the people who had to carry it?” Pause. Use silence productively. This question surfaces the lived experience that anchors the entire unit.

On the Five Principles: Work through these sequentially. Each builds on the previous. Do not allow leaders to skip to SCARF or ACE-IT without first establishing the foundational logic. Suggested section time: 45–60 minutes.

parts.title: 1.1 — The Human Terrain of Strategy Execution
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1

The Functional Bias Problem: Ask leaders to honestly name their primary perspective. The CFO thinks in capital efficiency. The COO in delivery flow. The CHRO in capability. None is wrong — but when these operate without deliberate integration, strategy fragments invisibly. Suggested time: 10–12 minutes.
Key facilitation question: “When your leadership team last debated a strategic priority — were you all interpreting the same data from the same perspective? Or from the perspective of your function?”
content: Strategy enters an organisation through the people responsible for interpreting and acting on it. Before strategy becomes operational activity, it passes through two human filters:
How individuals interpret what strategy means. Shaped by professional expertise, mental shortcuts, past experience, and risk perception.
How individuals experience the strategy. Shapes engagement energy, morale, friction load, psychological safety, and values alignment.
Whether strategy produces clarity or confusion, commitment or compliance, momentum or hesitation. Execution begins inside the human system.

The deeper challenge behind execution friction: Strategy is fundamentally a human interpretation problem. The Functional Bias Problem reveals that organisations do not interpret strategy as a single, shared reality. When perspectives diverge, even highly capable executives can unintentionally pull the organisation in different directions.

parts.title: 1.2 — The Five Principles of Aligning Heart & Mind
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2

Pacing: Open each principle card and read the insight aloud before inviting reflection. Do not let the group race through. Principle 2 (Misalignment Fragments Effort) generates the most immediate recognition — use it as a pivot.
After all five: “Which principle describes the most critical gap in your leadership team right now? Choose one.” The choice itself is diagnostic. Suggested time: 15–18 minutes.
content: The human entry point of execution. Alignment of the mind (cognition) and heart (emotion) is the first execution system.

Cognitive alignment focuses on making biases visible so they can be managed deliberately. In practice: identify dominant decision biases at executive level, name how those biases shape the S2R® process, establish shared decision principles that counter predictable distortions.

Emotional alignment requires naming the current emotional state through which strategy is being experienced. Leaders operate from a dominant state of being (Joy, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Disgust, Surprise). Each state influences engagement energy, morale drain, friction load, psychological safety, and values alignment.
➤ Facilitation insight: Ask leaders to name the dominant emotion in their current team right now. If they cannot name it, they cannot manage it — and it will manage them.
The cost of ignoring the human system. When interpretation and emotional experience are not aligned, effort begins to fragment. Everyone remains active, yet the organisation moves with split effort.
Intent mutates as it travels downward. Frontline execution bears little resemblance to boardroom intent.
60–80% of leadership time spent re-explaining, correcting, realigning. Leaders are patching.
People comply outwardly but withdraw inwardly. Looks like cooperation. Feels like exhaustion.
Data: Low-alignment organisations experience 41% lower productivity and 48% higher turnover. This drift is dangerous because it is gradual, rationalised, and expensive (Gallup; PMI).

Alignment rarely emerges naturally. It must be intentionally designed through structured interventions that make interpretation and emotional climate visible. Two diagnostic assessments support this design:

Surfaces psychological tendencies influencing executive decision-making. Dimensions: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Emotional Stability, Values Alignment, Learning Orientation. Available on demand — excel or HTML format with facilitated report generation.

Identifies the prevailing state of being across six core emotional categories: Joy, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Disgust, Surprise. Allows leaders to stabilise engagement before demanding execution. Available on demand.
➤ Facilitation insight: These assessments are diagnostic tools. Their power lies in the conversation they generate. Frame them as leadership mirrors.

Reactions to strategic change follow predictable psychological patterns. The SCARF Model (David Rock) explains five social conditions that trigger emotional responses during change. The human brain processes social change using the same threat circuitry as physical danger — any new goal, system, or way of working is evaluated emotionally before it is evaluated rationally.

The five SCARF triggers are explored in detail in the next section. The SCARF Tool is available on demand for leaders who want to monitor observable behaviours and proactively strengthen their alignment of heart and mind.
➤ Facilitation insight: The power of SCARF lies in the recognition. When a leader can name which trigger is driving resistance, they can address the root cause.
Execution Must Be Visible in Behaviour

Strategic alignment ultimately becomes visible through behaviour. Without observable behaviour, alignment remains theoretical. With behavioural standards, alignment becomes visible, measurable, and sustainable.

The ACE-IT Framework defines five universally desired behaviours: Accountability, Commitment, Engagement, Integrity, Transparency. These behaviours are independent of an organisation’s stated values — they represent the minimum behavioural standard for any leadership team serious about execution. Explored in detail in section 1.4.

➤ Facilitation insight: Ask leaders: “If someone external observed your team for one week, which ACE-IT behaviour would they see most clearly? Which would be absent?” The honest answer is a diagnostic.

parts.title: 1.3 — The SCARF Model: Five Triggers of Human Resistance
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3
On pacing: Open each SCARF card and read the trigger question aloud. Then pause: “In your last major strategy implementation — which of these triggers did you observe most? How did you know?”
Key distinction: The SCARF triggers activate universally. Leaders who manage it well are distinguished by awareness and deliberate counter-strategy. Suggested time: 12–15 minutes.
SCARF Tool

Available on demand for leaders who want to actively monitor observable behaviours during strategy discussions or change initiatives. Helps identify the underlying social concerns influencing reactions — enabling leaders to adjust their approach in real time.
content: Expand each trigger to explore what activates it, how it shows up in behaviour, its execution impact, and the counter-strategy that addresses it.
New leaders • New KPIs exposing performance • New systems shifting expertise • Changed reporting lines
Defensive behaviour • Undermining decisions • Withholding information or cooperation
⚠ Execution: Political friction • Slowed decisions • Misalignment masked as professionalism
➤ Counter: Explicitly acknowledge existing credibility. Involve senior leaders in co-designing new structures — status is protected when people have agency in the change.
“Do I know what success looks like?”
New goals • Ambiguous ownership • Changing metrics or timelines • Shifting review processes
Repeated clarification requests • Delay disguised as “waiting for alignment” • Reversion to old habits
⚠ Execution: Loss of momentum • Paralysis under pressure • Risk avoidance
➤ Counter: Create visible milestones early. The brain seeks pattern — give it enough structure to move without removing all ambiguity.
“Am I losing control of my work?”
New systems • Standardised processes • Centralised decision rights • Increased oversight or reporting
Passive compliance • Minimal effort delivery • Resistance through bureaucracy
⚠ Execution: Low engagement energy • Mechanical execution • Fragile performance
➤ Counter: Standardise the what and offer bounded choice on the how. Bounded choice preserves autonomy while honouring the mandate.
Team restructuring • New leaders or external hires • Cross-functional initiatives • Remote or hybrid shifts
Silo behaviour • Reduced collaboration • Guarded communication
⚠ Execution: Trust erosion • Coordination breakdown • Rework and duplication
➤ Counter: Create visible connection rituals during transitions. People need to feel part of the tribe before they will share resources or risk vulnerability.
Uneven workload • Selective enforcement of rules • Inconsistent rewards • Unclear decision rationale
Cynicism • Gossip replacing dialogue • Emotional withdrawal
⚠ Execution: Values misalignment • Morale drain • Cultural decay
➤ Counter: Proactively explain rationale behind decisions — especially asymmetric ones. Transparency about trade-offs is perceived as fairness even when outcomes differ.

parts.title: 1.4 — ACE-IT: The Observable Behaviour Standard
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4
Key framing: ACE-IT is a behavioural standard, independent of the organisation’s stated values. It describes the minimum visible behaviours required for strategic alignment to be real and visible.
After all five: “If you audited your last leadership review against these five behaviours — where would you find the biggest gap between the ideal and the observable?” Suggested time: 10–12 minutes.
content: Taking full ownership for results. Acknowledging missteps and driving corrective action.
Defines clear ownership • Acknowledges missteps • Holds self and others to measurable standards
✓ Observable: Commitments tracked • Reviews end with named owners • “We missed it, here’s the fix” language common
Staying anchored to agreed strategic intent even when pressure rises. Following through despite discomfort.
Aligns daily choices to long-term direction • Protects priorities from noise • Closes loops they open
✓ Observable: Strategic priorities stay consistent • Leaders decline non-strategic work • Promises kept visibly
Actively involving self and others in sense-making, dialogue, and execution. Listening to understand.
Invites participation and dissent • Connects roles to purpose • Creates two-way dialogue
✓ Observable: Team meetings are two-way • Feedback loops visible • People quote the shared “why”
Acting consistently with values, facts, and truth — even when inconvenient. Declaring conflicts of interest early.
Says what is true, even when it is hard • Uses data to support choices • References values in trade-offs
✓ Observable: Evidence cited before decisions • Values referenced in hard choices • Teams trust word matches deed
Making reasoning, progress, and constraints visible to all stakeholders. Sharing challenges openly.
Communicates decisions with rationale • Documents choices and lessons • Shares progress including setbacks
✓ Observable: Dashboards updated regularly • Decisions logged and accessible • “No surprises” culture evident

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Does Heart & Mind Alignment Determine Execution Outcomes?
sections.sub: Ignition Point · Within the Strategy2Results® process, Aligning Hearts and Minds functions as the ignition point of execution — the moment where strategy transitions from a document describing intent into a system capable of producing movement.
slo: Explain why shared understanding and commitment convert strategy into execution.
Distinguish execution driven by commitment from execution driven by compliance.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2 · Intelligence

Section intent: Move from describing the concept of alignment to understanding its strategic necessity. Leaders must understand why this is the mechanical conversion point of strategy. This section should create a shift from intellectual understanding to operational conviction.

The energy analogy: The Potential vs. Kinetic Energy logic is highly effective with CXO-level audiences. Engineers, finance leaders, and operators all recognise this from their domain. Use it as an anchor before moving to the compliance/commitment distinction. Suggested section time: 25–30 minutes.

parts.title: 2.1 — The Ignition Point of Strategy Execution
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2.1

On the ignition metaphor: An ignition point is where fuel becomes power. A strategy document is stored potential. The moment a person decides “This matters to me” is when kinetic energy begins. Without that moment, the fuel stays fuel.

Discussion prompt: “Think of a time when you personally chose to go beyond compliance and genuinely committed to a strategic direction. What caused that shift? What would it take to create that same shift in your team?” Suggested time: 8–10 minutes.
content: A strategy document contains strategic potential. It articulates direction, ambition, and possibility. However, potential by definition represents energy at rest. For strategic potential to convert into kinetic energy — movement, execution, and results — human action must occur. No system executes itself.

Execution begins the moment an individual decides: “This matters to me. I am willing to invest energy in making this succeed.” Until that moment occurs across the organisation, strategy remains theoretical. Aligning Hearts and Minds activates the human energy required to convert intention into action. This is the ignition point.

Without this ignition point, strategy remains defined but not delivered. With it, the organisation shifts from supervised effort to self-driven momentum — the strategic payoff that makes alignment the highest-leverage leadership intervention available.

parts.title: 2.2 — Three Foundational Logics
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2.2

Logic II (Compliance vs. Commitment) typically generates the highest impact with CXO audiences. Leaders recognise compliance-driven execution immediately — they have managed it and been frustrated by it. Ask: “How much of your leadership time is currently spent enforcing compliance?” The honest answer is usually sobering. Suggested time: 12–15 minutes.
content: I. Potential vs. Kinetic Energy Logic

A strategy document is strategic potential — energy at rest. For it to become kinetic energy (movement, execution, results), a human decision must activate it. The alignment of heart and mind is precisely the conversion mechanism. Every day that decision is not made is a day strategic potential sits unused. The organisation does not move until people decide to move it. Leadership cannot shortcut this decision — it can only create the conditions for it.

People act because authority requires it, rules enforce it, or systems monitor it. Produces visible output short-term. Requires continuous supervision. Creates hidden costs: leadership time consumed by follow-ups, teams dependent on instruction, decision-making slows as control increases. Mechanical and brittle.

People act because they understand strategic intent, believe the direction is meaningful, and feel personal ownership. Generates behaviours compliance cannot sustain: discretionary effort, adaptive problem-solving, resilience when conditions change. Execution continues even when leaders are not present.
III. The Strategic Payoff of Alignment

When both cognition and emotion are aligned: people act with ownership, coordination improves across functions, and leaders spend less time correcting and more time advancing strategy. This shift reduces rework, lowers escalation, and preserves leadership capacity for decisions that truly require executive attention. Aligning Hearts and Minds is the mechanical conversion point where strategic potential becomes strategic movement.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Are the Alignment Hot Zones Across the Organisation?
sections.sub: The Alignment Brigade · The COMPASS framework identifies seven High Flammable Zones where human interpretation, emotional climate, and behaviour directly influence strategic outcomes. These are the leverage points — and the danger zones.
slo: Recognise where interpretation, emotional climate and behaviour most strengthen or weaken alignment.
Identify the warning signals that alignment is escalating into crisis.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3 · Extrapolating

Section intent: Make the alignment concept specific and organisationally urgent. Leaders must finish this section knowing where their most significant alignment risks live, in named domains of their enterprise.

Diagnostic exercise: Before revealing the COMPASS narratives, ask participants to independently rate their organisation on each domain (1 = strong alignment, 5 = severe misalignment). Then compare ratings across the leadership team. Divergent ratings are themselves diagnostic. Suggested section time: 35–45 minutes.

parts.title: 3.1 — The COMPASS Framework: Seven High Flammable Zones
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3.1

On the COMPASS cards: Invite leaders to click the domain they rated highest risk first. Then ask the group: “Who has a different view? Where does your assessment diverge?” Divergence in the room is itself a signal — name it explicitly.

Key distinction: High Flammables are leverage points — dangerous, but early intervention stabilises them. Burning Platforms are what happens when leverage points are ignored. The COMPASS diagnostic is about catching zones before they ignite. Suggested time: 18–22 minutes.
content: Click each COMPASS domain to explore the signal narrative, how it appears when lit, and the facilitation question that drives early intervention.

The most dangerous fire in any organisation is the quiet combustion when leaders believe they are aligned but are navigating by different compasses. Clarity of Strategic Direction is whether people can describe the strategy in the same language, connect it to daily decisions, and hold it steady under pressure.

When this signal flares: confidence in meetings, confusion in corridors. Priorities multiply. Trade-offs are avoided. Frontline execution diverges from boardroom intent when the destination was never made unambiguous enough to follow.

Executives presenting polished strategies that fracture the moment they leave the room. Multiple competing priorities in different functions. Leaders spending time re-explaining decisions that should already be settled.
⚠ Signal lit: “Everyone has a different version of what we said.”
➤ Facilitation question: “Can every person in this room describe the top three strategic priorities in the same order, using the same language? Try it now.”

Alignment is coordinated behaviour outside the room. Leaders declare alignment after a planning session, observe nodding in forums, and interpret absence of challenge as shared commitment. They are often wrong. True alignment is only visible in behaviour.
When this signal ignites, it burns slowly and spreads widely. Silos deepen. Functions execute their own version of the strategy. The informal system quietly undermines the formal one.

Agreements reached in meetings relitigated through resource approvals and parallel conversations. Initiatives requiring cross-functional collaboration consistently stall. Senior arbitration required for decisions that should be self-coordinating.
⚠ Signal lit: “We agreed on this — why is it not happening?”
➤ Facilitation question: “Where in your organisation do decisions made at the top not survive the journey to implementation? What sits between the decision and the delivery?”

Strategy fails in the gap between what leaders decide and what managers actually enforce, measure, and hold accountable. Management Discipline is the signal that tells you whether the operating rhythm — reviews, escalation norms, accountability structures, governance forums — is a genuine engine of delivery or an elaborate performance of oversight.
When this signal flares, performance reviews recycle the same issues without resolution. The same gaps appear in consecutive cycles and are explained and left uncorrected.

Accountability is diffuse — owned collectively, which means owned by no one. Leaders tolerate persistent underperformance. The culture has decided that explanation is an acceptable substitute for consequence.
⚠ Signal lit: “We keep discussing the same issues with no resolution.”
➤ Facilitation question: “In your last three performance reviews, what was the single most recurring issue? Has it been resolved, or has it been re-explained?”

Organisations frequently approve strategies that their people are not yet equipped to deliver. The People & Capability signal is alight when there is a meaningful distance between the skills, capacity, and engagement required and what the organisation actually has available.

This signal is particularly dangerous because it is slow-burning and easy to rationalise. Leaders attribute execution failures to process or strategy when the root cause is a capability system never designed to carry the weight being placed on it.

Middle managers stretched beyond bandwidth. Succession plans that exist as documents but not operational reality. Engagement scores declining while leadership describes culture as resilient. Key talent exiting quietly. Institutional knowledge walking out the door.
⚠ Signal lit: “We have the strategy but not the people to execute it.”
➤ Facilitation question: “If you had to deliver your strategy with the team you have today — which specific capability gaps would most limit you? When did you last name those gaps explicitly?”

An organisation’s true strategy is found in its budget. When this signal ignites, there is a visible gap between what leadership declares as strategic and what gets funded, staffed, and protected when decisions become difficult.

Legacy spend continues by inertia. New priorities are approved in language but starved in practice. The longer resources misalign with stated direction, the more credibility erodes, and the harder it becomes to mobilise genuine commitment behind any priority.

Stated priorities and funded priorities are clearly different. Strategy decks bear no resemblance to budget allocation. “Strategic” initiatives consistently underfunded or deferred. Leaders handed responsibility without resources to honour it.
⚠ Signal lit: “We say this is a priority but the resources tell a different story.”
➤ Facilitation question: “Look at your budget allocation. Does money follow the stated strategy? Where is the gap between declared priority and funded priority?”

Markets shift. Customer needs evolve. Competitive dynamics change faster than planning cycles. The Sensing & Adaptation signal measures whether the organisation is genuinely learning from what is happening around it — or whether it is processing information selectively, defending existing plans, and mistaking activity for responsiveness.
The deeper danger is cultural — when leaders learn that raising uncomfortable signals carries social cost, the organisation gradually loses its early warning system entirely.

Customer data reviewed but not acted on. Market shifts acknowledged then filed away. Leaders defending forecasts the evidence no longer supports. Early warning signals dismissed as noise. The organisation confuses having a strategy with having the right strategy.
⚠ Signal lit: “We knew this was coming, but we didn’t adapt fast enough.”
➤ Facilitation question: “What is one market or customer signal your organisation is receiving that is not yet reflected in your strategic plan? What would it take to act on it?”

A new strategy running through an old machine will always produce the same result. Systems & Execution asks the hardest question: is the organisation actually built to deliver what it has committed to, in its architecture? Does the operating model match the strategic priorities?

When this signal is lit, technology investments produce impressive demonstrations and negligible adoption. Operating models built for stability are asked to deliver agility. Leaders sense something fundamental is misaligned but reach for tactical interventions when what is required is a willingness to redesign the machine.

The organisation invests in transformation while being structurally configured to resist it. Structural ambiguities create friction compounding with every execution cycle. Leaders sense misalignment but add governance layers, urgency, or communication, and leave the structure unchanged.
⚠ Signal lit: “The structure is working against the strategy.”
➤ Facilitation question: “Is your current operating model designed for the strategy you have now — or for a strategy you had two years ago? What would redesigning the machine actually require?”

parts.title: 3.2 — From High Flammables to Burning Platforms
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3.2

On the escalation threshold: High Flammable Zones are pressure points with high leverage. They become Burning Platforms only when alignment is consistently absent and the zone crosses a tipping point. Ask: “Which of your COMPASS domains is closest to that threshold right now?”

Enterprise COMPASS Screening Tool: Available on demand. Helps teams move from vague alignment concerns to clear diagnosis and targeted intervention. Recommended for use at strategy reviews and execution forums. Suggested time: 8–10 minutes.
Enterprise COMPASS Screening Tool

Available on demand for structured diagnostic baseline. Used regularly during strategy reviews, execution forums, or leadership discussions to identify which zones are approaching the escalation threshold before they cross it. Converts vague “alignment concerns” into specific diagnosis and targeted intervention.
content: Organisational leverage points. When alignment is strong: rapid clarity, coordinated effort, compounding momentum. When alignment is weak: distorted interpretation, defensive behaviour, multiplying friction.
✓ Early intervention stabilises the zone and converts it into a performance amplifier.

What a High Flammable becomes when misalignment persists and crosses the escalation threshold. By this point, execution breakdown is visible and costly. Reactive interventions cost exponentially more than proactive alignment would have.
⚠ The same zone that was manageable as a leverage point becomes a crisis requiring systemic rebuilding.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.h2: How Aligning Heart & Mind Creates Collective Intelligence
sections.sub: The Converging Zone · The executive team enters the Converging Zone, where individual functional perspectives integrate into a shared leadership interpretation. At this point, the leadership team begins operating as a single leadership system, stabilising all seven COMPASS domains.
slo: Explain how individual alignment responsibilities combine into a coherent enterprise interpretation.
Recognise where gaps in role alignment create enterprise vulnerability.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4 · Integration

Section intent: Lift the focus from individual alignment to systemic leadership alignment. The Converging Zone is where individual functional expertise becomes coordinated leadership judgement. Without this, the organisation receives multiple interpretations of strategy, causing instability across all seven COMPASS domains.

On the role grid: Ask each leader to click their own role card first. Then: “Do you recognise this description? Is this how your team experiences your alignment contribution?” Then invite leaders to look at each other’s cards. This is particularly powerful when the full CXO team is in the room. Suggested section time: 30–40 minutes.

parts.title: 4.1 — The Converging Zone: What Collective Intelligence Creates
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4.1

Two states exercise: Ask leaders to identify which state their organisation is currently closer to. Then: “What is the single most important convergence you need to achieve before your next major strategy initiative?” Suggested time: 8–10 minutes.
content: Direction remains clear across all layers
✓ One coherent signal across the organisation. COMPASS domains become leverage points for performance.
⚠ Multiple conflicting signals. Leverage zones become sources of execution friction.

parts.title: 4.2 — Collective Intelligence Across the Leadership Team
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4.2

Key facilitation: After each leader has reviewed their own role, invite them to look at the role most adjacent to theirs. Ask: “What is the most important alignment conversation you need to have with that role in the next 30 days?” The answer frequently becomes a direct post-session commitment. Suggested time: 15–18 minutes.
content: Click a role to explore how each CXO function contributes to Collective Intelligence and which COMPASS domains it most directly activates.

Integrates all seven COMPASS domains into one coherent strategic narrative. Ensures direction, priorities, and trade-offs are communicated with one leadership voice. The CEO’s primary alignment responsibility is preventing the “Chinese Whispers” effect by keeping the strategic story intact as it moves through the organisation.
When the CEO’s alignment is absent or inconsistent, all other roles struggle to converge — the COMPASS framework loses its anchor point.

Ensures capital allocation and financial discipline reinforce strategic intent and concentrate resources on the agreed priorities. The CFO’s alignment responsibility is making the budget reflect the stated strategy — and having the courage to make trade-offs visible when they arise.
When the CFO’s alignment is absent, resources follow inertia, and the credibility of strategic priorities collapses.

Converts strategy into operational flow, ensuring execution routines, coordination, and hand-offs move the organisation forward. The COO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring the operating system is configured for the current strategy.
When COO alignment is absent, execution machinery runs efficiently but in the wrong direction.

Aligns leadership behaviour, capability development, and organisational trust with the strategic direction. The CHRO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring the human system has the capacity, engagement, and psychological safety to carry the strategy forward.
When CHRO alignment is absent, strategy consistently exceeds the human system’s capacity to carry it.

Aligns technology architecture and data capability with the organisation’s strategic priorities and future operating model. The CTO/CIO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring technology investments actually change how the organisation works.
When CTO/CIO alignment is absent, technology investments produce demonstrations with no capability shift.

Aligns market positioning and brand promise with the organisation’s operational ability to deliver. The CMO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring that demand created externally can be fulfilled internally — and that the brand promise is one the organisation can keep consistently.
When CMO alignment is absent, market signals are disconnected from strategic direction, and brand promises outpace operational reality.

Aligns revenue generation and customer growth strategies with enterprise positioning and operational capacity. The CCO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring all deals strengthen the organisation’s distinctive positioning — that all revenue is strategic revenue.
When CCO alignment is absent, growth strategies create internal incoherence that compounds over time.

Ensures procurement decisions strengthen operational capability and reinforce strategic priorities. The CPO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring cost efficiency decisions serve the customer’s end-game and the strategy’s priorities.
When CPO alignment is absent, procurement optimises for cost at the expense of strategic capability.

Aligns enterprise risk interpretation so that strategic initiatives operate within a shared risk appetite framework. The CRO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring risk assessment enables strategic ambition — and that risk tolerance is consistently interpreted across all functions.
When CRO alignment is absent, risk appetite becomes function-by-function interpretation, creating asymmetric exposure.

Maintains the integrity of the strategic narrative as it moves from formulation into execution across the organisation. The CSO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring the strategy survives the transition from idea to implementation — that strategic intent does not mutate as it moves through the organisation.
When CSO alignment is absent, the strategic narrative fragments and different layers execute different versions of the strategy.

sections.label: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
sections.h2: Building Collective Intelligence Through Shared Interpretation
sections.sub: Application · This exercise highlights how Collective Intelligence emerges when leaders understand each other’s alignment responsibilities. The goal: move from individual interpretations to a shared understanding of how roles jointly stabilise all seven COMPASS domains.
slo: Formulate a shared interpretation of how leadership roles connect to support coordinated action.
Demonstrate commitment through a behavioural change that strengthens collective alignment.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5 · Application

Timing: Step 1 is individual — 12–15 minutes. Step 2 is paired exchange — 15–20 minutes. Step 3 is plenary synthesis — 20–25 minutes. Do not rush Steps 1–2. The quality of the plenary depends entirely on the depth of individual reflection and peer dialogue that precedes it.

Facilitation principle: Your role in the plenary is to name patterns. When leaders disagree about connectivity, name it explicitly: “That disagreement tells us something important about how alignment responsibilities are currently experienced in this team.”
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Step 1

Briefing: Each person works independently. They complete the table for their own role first, then for two closely related roles. The “How We Create Collective Intelligence” column must go beyond job description — it should describe the alignment mechanism the role provides to the organisation.

Watch for: Participants who list tasks; push them to name alignment contributions. Redirect: “That’s what you do — what happens to the organisation’s alignment when you do it well? And when you don’t?”
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Participants complete the map for their own role and two closely related roles. Circulate and check that each row names a specific COMPASS domain and a concrete collaboration behaviour.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Step 2

Process: Each leader shares their table with the colleague(s) whose role they selected. Three exchange questions: (1) Do you agree with how I described your alignment contribution? (2) How else do you create Collective Intelligence that I missed? (3) Where do our interpretations diverge?

Key facilitation move: Where leaders disagree, do not resolve it. Name it explicitly: “That disagreement is diagnostic. It tells you something about how these roles are currently experienced in the organisation.”
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Pair participants from closely related roles. Allow five minutes per person, then ask each pair where their interpretations diverged. Treat divergence as diagnostic and leave it unresolved.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Step 3

Synthesis question: “Looking at all the tables in the room — which COMPASS domain appears most frequently as underactivated or poorly understood? That is your team’s most critical alignment vulnerability.”

Closing commitment: Each leader names one specific behavioural change in the next 30 days to strengthen their alignment contribution. Make these visible — write them on the board or capture them centrally. Follow up at the next leadership forum.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
Facilitate the group synthesis: the most underactivated COMPASS domain, shared strengths and connectivity gaps. Close by asking each participant to read one 30-day behavioural commitment aloud.

parts.title: Unit Summary
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Unit Summary

Closing the unit: Use this summary to close the session, to brief sponsors or observers beforehand, or to re-anchor the group at the start of a later session. Reserve the final five minutes for one pointed question: “Which COMPASS domain is this team most likely rating too generously — and which executive role has quietly stopped carrying its alignment responsibility there?” It is also the reference point for connecting this unit to what follows — Performance Management Setup and the translation of strategy into individual accountability across the enterprise.
content: This session was about the human conditions that decide whether a strategy ever moves. We have all watched sound strategies stall because the people meant to execute it never aligned in how they interpreted it or whether they were committed to it. Aligning Hearts & Minds treated execution as first a human problem: strategy moves through people before it moves through systems.
Here is a recap of how we moved from fragmented functional interpretations to a single, committed leadership signal.
1 — Awareness: Strategy Enters Through Two Human Filters

We began with the What. Strategy enters through Cognition (Mind), how each leader interprets it, and Emotion (Heart), how each leader experiences it. When these diverge across a team, the Functional Bias Problem fragments execution into competing interpretations. The unit established Five Principles:
Strategy Moves Through People — direction is carried by interpretation.
Misalignment Fragments Effort — surfacing as Chinese Whispers, Clarification Debt, and Silent Disengagement.
Alignment Must Be Designed — diagnosed with the OCEAVL Assessment and the Emotional Climate Assessment.
Human Reactions Are Predictable — the SCARF Model (Status, Certainty, Autonomy, Relatedness, Fairness) trips the same threat circuitry as physical danger.
Execution Must Be Visible in Behaviour — the ACE-IT standard: Accountability, Commitment, Engagement, Integrity, Transparency.
2 — Intelligence: Why Alignment Is the Ignition Point

This stage explored the Why. Heart & Mind alignment is the ignition point that converts strategic potential energy (the document at rest) into kinetic energy (movement and results). Three logics make the stakes operational:
Potential vs Kinetic Energy — the organisation does not move until people decide to move it.

Compliance vs Commitment — compliance (Mind only) yields short-term output but is mechanical and consumes leadership time; commitment (Mind + Heart) generates discretionary effort, adaptive problem-solving, and resilience when leaders are not present.
The Strategic Payoff — aligned teams act with ownership, coordinate across functions, and free leaders to advance strategy.
Next, the Where. Misalignment concentrates in seven High Flammable Zones, mapped by the COMPASS framework:

Each domain carries a signal narrative and a diagnostic question, and is rated 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment). A lit zone is either a High Flammable — a live leverage point — or a Burning Platform, escalated and consuming resources. Mapping where the signals are lit tells leaders where alignment work earns the highest return.

The session culminated in the Converging Zone, where functional interpretations integrate into a shared leadership signal and the team begins operating as a single leadership system. Each CXO role carries a distinct alignment responsibility, mapped to two primary COMPASS activations:
CEO — anchors Clarity of Strategic Direction and Organisational Alignment
CFO / CPO — activate Allocation of Resources
COO / CTO / CRO — drive Systems & Execution
CMO / CSO — maintain Clarity and Sensing & Adaptation
When any role drops its responsibility, the COMPASS framework loses an anchor and the rest cannot fully converge. Collective Intelligence is the combined signal.

Aligned hearts and minds turn a strategy from a document the organisation has read into a direction the organisation is willing to move on — the human foundation for Performance Management Setup and the translation of strategy into individual accountability across the enterprise.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Before any strategy can be executed, it must travel through people. People arrive at every strategy meeting carrying a personality profile, emotional defaults, and personal motives that determine how much energy they will invest in the organisation’s goals.
slo: Examine how functional expertise, cognitive bias and emotion shape the interpretation of strategy.
Recognise the triggers of resistance and the behaviours that sustain alignment.

parts.title: 1.1 — The Human Terrain of Strategy Execution
content: Strategy enters an organisation through the people responsible for interpreting and acting on it. Before strategy becomes operational activity, it passes through two human filters:
How individuals interpret what strategy means. Shaped by professional expertise, mental shortcuts, past experience, and risk perception.
How individuals experience the strategy. Shapes engagement energy, morale, friction load, psychological safety, and values alignment.
Whether strategy produces clarity or confusion, commitment or compliance. Execution begins inside the human system.

The deeper challenge behind execution friction: Strategy is fundamentally a human interpretation problem. The Functional Bias Problem reveals that when perspectives diverge, even highly capable executives can unintentionally pull the organisation in different directions.
In your current role, which filter (Mind or Heart) tends to shape your first response to a new strategic priority? What are the implications?
prompts: ✎ Reflection In your current role, which filter (Mind or Heart) tends to shape your first response to a new strategic priority? What are the implications?

parts.title: 1.2 — The Five Principles of Aligning Heart & Mind
content: The human entry point of execution. Alignment of the mind (cognition) and heart (emotion) is the first execution system.

Cognitive alignment focuses on making biases visible so they can be managed deliberately. Emotional alignment requires naming the current state through which strategy is being experienced. Leaders operating from Joy, Commitment, and Confidence invest very differently from those operating from Fear, Uncertainty, or Disengagement.
➤ Insight: Can you name the dominant emotion your team is carrying into the current strategy? If you cannot name it, you cannot manage it.

When interpretation and emotional experience diverge, effort begins to fragment. The three most visible consequences: Chinese Whispers (intent mutates downward), Clarification Debt (leadership time consumed by re-explanation), Silent Disengagement (compliance without commitment).
Data: Low-alignment organisations experience 41% lower productivity and 48% higher turnover (Gallup; PMI). This drift is gradual, rationalised, and expensive.

Alignment rarely emerges naturally. It must be intentionally designed. Two diagnostic assessments support this: the OCEAVL Assessment (surfaces psychological tendencies influencing decision-making) and the Emotional Climate Assessment (identifies the prevailing state of being through which strategy is currently being experienced). Both available on demand.
➤ Insight: These assessments are leadership mirrors. Their power lies in the conversation they generate.

Reactions to strategic change follow predictable psychological patterns. The SCARF Model explains five social conditions that trigger emotional responses during change. The human brain processes social change using the same threat circuitry as physical danger — any new goal, system, or way of working is evaluated emotionally before it is evaluated rationally.
➤ Insight: When you can name which SCARF trigger is driving resistance, you can address the root cause.
Execution Must Be Visible in Behaviour

Without observable behaviour, alignment remains theoretical. The ACE-IT Framework defines five universally desired behaviours: Accountability, Commitment, Engagement, Integrity, Transparency — independent of an organisation’s stated values. They represent the minimum behavioural standard for any leadership team serious about execution.
➤ Insight: If someone external observed your team for one week, which ACE-IT behaviour would they see most clearly? Which would be absent?
Which of the Five Principles describes the most critical gap in your leadership team right now? What is the evidence for this?
prompts: ✎ Reflection Which of the Five Principles describes the most critical gap in your leadership team right now? What is the evidence for this?

parts.title: 1.3 — The SCARF Model: Five Triggers of Human Resistance
content: New leaders • New KPIs exposing performance • New systems shifting expertise • Changed reporting lines
Defensive behaviour • Undermining decisions • Withholding information or cooperation
⚠ Execution: Political friction • Slowed decisions • Misalignment masked as professionalism
➤ Counter: Explicitly acknowledge existing credibility. Involve senior leaders in co-designing new structures.
“Do I know what success looks like?”
New goals • Ambiguous ownership • Changing metrics or timelines • Shifting review processes
Repeated clarification requests • Delay disguised as “waiting for alignment” • Reversion to old habits
⚠ Execution: Loss of momentum • Paralysis under pressure • Risk avoidance
➤ Counter: Create visible milestones early. Give the brain enough structure to move without removing all ambiguity.
“Am I losing control of my work?”
New systems • Standardised processes • Centralised decision rights • Increased oversight or reporting
Passive compliance • Minimal effort delivery • Resistance through bureaucracy
⚠ Execution: Low engagement energy • Mechanical execution • Fragile performance
➤ Counter: Standardise the what and offer bounded choice on the how. Bounded choice preserves autonomy while honouring the mandate.
Team restructuring • New leaders or external hires • Cross-functional initiatives • Remote or hybrid shifts
Silo behaviour • Reduced collaboration • Guarded communication
⚠ Execution: Trust erosion • Coordination breakdown • Rework and duplication
➤ Counter: Create visible connection rituals during transitions. People share resources only when they feel part of the tribe.
Uneven workload • Selective enforcement • Inconsistent rewards • Unclear decision rationale
Cynicism • Gossip replacing dialogue • Emotional withdrawal
⚠ Execution: Values misalignment • Morale drain • Cultural decay
➤ Counter: Explain rationale behind asymmetric decisions proactively. Transparency about trade-offs is perceived as fairness.
Which SCARF trigger is most frequently activated in your organisation during strategy implementation? What is the observable evidence? What counter-strategy would address the root cause?
prompts: ✎ Reflection Which SCARF trigger is most frequently activated in your organisation during strategy implementation? What is the observable evidence? What counter-strategy would address the root cause?

parts.title: 1.4 — ACE-IT: The Observable Behaviour Standard
content: Taking full ownership for results. Acknowledging missteps and driving corrective action.
Defines clear ownership • Acknowledges missteps • Holds self and others to measurable standards
✓ Observable: Commitments tracked • Reviews end with named owners • “We missed it, here’s the fix” language common
Staying anchored to agreed strategic intent even when pressure rises. Following through despite discomfort.
Aligns daily choices to long-term direction • Protects priorities from noise • Closes loops they open
✓ Observable: Strategic priorities stay consistent • Leaders decline non-strategic work • Promises kept visibly
Actively involving self and others in sense-making, dialogue, and execution. Listening to understand.
Invites participation and dissent • Connects roles to purpose • Creates two-way dialogue
✓ Observable: Team meetings are two-way • Feedback loops visible • People quote the shared “why”
Acting consistently with values, facts, and truth — even when inconvenient.
Says what is true, even when it is hard • Uses data to support choices • References values in trade-offs
✓ Observable: Evidence cited before decisions • Values referenced in hard choices • Teams trust word matches deed
Making reasoning, progress, and constraints visible to all stakeholders. Sharing challenges openly.
Communicates decisions with rationale • Documents choices and lessons • Shares progress including setbacks
✓ Observable: Dashboards updated regularly • Decisions logged and accessible • “No surprises” culture evident

If you audited your last leadership review against the ACE-IT behaviours — where would you find the biggest gap between the ideal and the observable? What one behavioural change would create the most impact?
prompts: ✎ Reflection If you audited your last leadership review against the ACE-IT behaviours — where would you find the biggest gap between the ideal and the observable? What one behavioural change would create the most impact?

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why Does Heart & Mind Alignment Determine Execution Outcomes?
sections.sub: Within the Strategy2Results® process, Aligning Hearts and Minds functions as the ignition point of execution — the moment where strategy transitions from a document describing intent into a system capable of producing movement.
slo: Explain why shared understanding and commitment convert strategy into execution.
Distinguish execution driven by commitment from execution driven by compliance.

parts.title: 2.1 — The Ignition Point of Strategy Execution
content: A strategy document contains strategic potential. It articulates direction, ambition, and possibility. However, potential by definition represents energy at rest. For strategic potential to convert into kinetic energy — movement, execution, and results — human action must occur.

Execution begins the moment an individual decides: “This matters to me. I am willing to invest energy in making this succeed.” Until that moment occurs across the organisation, strategy remains theoretical. Aligning Hearts and Minds activates the human energy required to convert intention into action.
Think of a time when you personally chose to go beyond compliance and genuinely committed to a strategic direction. What caused that shift? What would it take to create that same shift in your team?
prompts: ✎ Reflection Think of a time when you personally chose to go beyond compliance and genuinely committed to a strategic direction. What caused that shift? What would it take to create that same shift in your team?

parts.title: 2.2 — Three Foundational Logics
content: I. Potential vs. Kinetic Energy Logic

A strategy document is strategic potential — energy at rest. For it to become kinetic energy, a human decision must activate it. Every day that decision is not made is a day strategic potential sits unused. The organisation does not move until people decide to move it.

People act because authority requires it. Produces visible output short-term. Requires continuous supervision. Creates hidden costs: leadership time consumed by follow-ups, decision-making slows as control increases. Mechanical and brittle.

People act because they understand intent, believe the direction is meaningful, and feel personal ownership. Generates discretionary effort, adaptive problem-solving, resilience when conditions change. Execution continues when leaders are not present.
III. The Strategic Payoff of Alignment

When both cognition and emotion are aligned: people act with ownership, coordination improves across functions, and leaders spend less time correcting and more time advancing strategy. Aligning Hearts and Minds is the mechanical conversion point where strategic potential becomes strategic movement.
How much of your current leadership time is spent enforcing compliance? What is the opportunity cost of this?
prompts: ✎ Reflection How much of your current leadership time is spent enforcing compliance? What is the opportunity cost of this?

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Are the Alignment Hot Zones Across the Organisation?
sections.sub: The COMPASS framework identifies seven High Flammable Zones where human interpretation, emotional climate, and behaviour directly influence strategic outcomes. These are the leverage points — and the danger zones.
slo: Recognise where interpretation, emotional climate and behaviour most strengthen or weaken alignment.
Identify the warning signals that alignment is escalating into crisis.

parts.title: 3.1 — The COMPASS Framework: Seven High Flammable Zones
content: Click each COMPASS domain to explore the signal narrative and the facilitation question that drives early intervention.

Clarity of Strategic Direction is whether people can describe the strategy in the same language, connect it to daily decisions, and hold it steady under pressure. When this signal flares: confidence in meetings, confusion in corridors. Priorities multiply and trade-offs are avoided.
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “Everyone has a different version of what we said.”
➤ Can every person in your leadership team describe the top three strategic priorities in the same order, using the same language? What would happen if you tested this now?

Alignment is coordinated behaviour outside the room. Leaders declare alignment after a planning session and interpret absence of challenge as shared commitment. True alignment is only visible in behaviour. When this signal ignites, silos deepen and functions execute their own version of the strategy.
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We agreed on this — why is it not happening?”
➤ Where in your organisation do decisions made at the top not survive the journey to implementation? What sits between the decision and the delivery?

Strategy fails in the gap between what leaders decide and what managers actually enforce, measure, and hold accountable. Management Discipline tells you whether the operating rhythm — reviews, escalation norms, accountability structures — is a genuine engine of delivery or an elaborate performance of oversight. When this signal flares, the same gaps appear in consecutive cycles and are explained and left uncorrected.
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We keep discussing the same issues with no resolution.”
➤ In your last three performance reviews, what was the single most recurring issue? Has it been resolved, or has it been re-explained?

Organisations frequently approve strategies that their people are not yet equipped to deliver. This signal is particularly dangerous because it is slow-burning and easy to rationalise. Leaders attribute execution failures to process or strategy when the root cause is a capability system never designed to carry the weight being placed on it.
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We have the strategy but not the people to execute it.”
➤ If you had to deliver your strategy with the team you have today — which specific capability gaps would most limit you? When did you last name those gaps explicitly?

An organisation’s true strategy is found in its budget. When this signal ignites, there is a visible gap between what leadership declares as strategic and what gets funded, staffed, and protected when decisions become difficult. Legacy spend continues by inertia while stated priorities are starved in practice.
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We say this is a priority but the resources tell a different story.”
➤ Look at your budget allocation. Does money follow the stated strategy? Where is the gap between declared priority and funded priority?

The Sensing & Adaptation signal measures whether the organisation is genuinely learning from what is happening around it — or whether it is processing information selectively and defending existing plans. The deeper danger: when raising uncomfortable signals carries social cost, the organisation gradually loses its early warning system entirely.
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “We knew this was coming, but we didn’t adapt fast enough.”
➤ What is one market or customer signal your organisation is receiving that is not yet reflected in your strategic plan? What would it take to act on it?

A new strategy running through an old machine will always produce the same result. Systems & Execution asks: is the organisation actually built to deliver what it has committed to, in its architecture? Does the operating model match the strategic priorities?
Rate your organisation in this domain: 1 (strong alignment) to 5 (severe misalignment).
⚠ Signal lit: “The structure is working against the strategy.”
➤ Is your current operating model designed for the strategy you have now — or for a strategy you had two years ago? What would redesigning the machine actually require?
Which domain did you rate highest risk? What is the observable evidence? Is it still a High Flammable or has it crossed to Burning Platform?
prompts: ✎ Reflection — COMPASS Diagnostic Which domain did you rate highest risk? What is the observable evidence? Is it still a High Flammable or has it crossed to Burning Platform?

parts.title: 3.2 — From High Flammables to Burning Platforms
content: Organisational leverage points. When alignment is strong: rapid clarity, coordinated effort, compounding momentum. When alignment is weak: distorted interpretation, defensive behaviour, multiplying friction.
✓ Early intervention stabilises the zone and converts it into a performance amplifier.

What a High Flammable becomes when misalignment persists and crosses the escalation threshold. By this point, execution breakdown is visible and costly. Reactive interventions cost exponentially more than proactive alignment would have.
⚠ The same zone that was manageable as a leverage point becomes a crisis requiring systemic rebuilding.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.h2: How Aligning Heart & Mind Creates Collective Intelligence
sections.sub: The executive team enters the Converging Zone, where individual functional perspectives integrate into a shared leadership interpretation. The leadership team begins operating as a single leadership system, stabilising all seven COMPASS domains.
slo: Explain how individual alignment responsibilities combine into a coherent enterprise interpretation.
Recognise where gaps in role alignment create enterprise vulnerability.

parts.title: 4.1 — The Converging Zone: What Collective Intelligence Creates
content: Direction remains clear across all layers
✓ One coherent signal across the organisation.
⚠ Multiple conflicting signals. Leverage zones become friction.
Which state is your organisation currently closer to? What is the single most important convergence you need to achieve before your next major strategy initiative?
prompts: ✎ Reflection Which state is your organisation currently closer to? What is the single most important convergence you need to achieve before your next major strategy initiative?

parts.title: 4.2 — Collective Intelligence Across the Leadership Team
content: Click your own role first. Then explore the roles most closely connected to yours.

Integrates all seven COMPASS domains into one coherent strategic narrative. Ensures direction, priorities, and trade-offs are communicated with one leadership voice. The CEO’s primary alignment responsibility is preventing the “Chinese Whispers” effect by keeping the strategic story intact as it moves through the organisation.
When absent: all other roles struggle to converge — the COMPASS framework loses its anchor point.

Ensures capital allocation and financial discipline reinforce strategic intent. The CFO’s alignment responsibility is making the budget reflect the stated strategy — and having the courage to make trade-offs visible when they arise.
When absent: resources follow inertia, and the credibility of strategic priorities collapses.

Converts strategy into operational flow, ensuring execution routines, coordination, and hand-offs move the organisation forward. The COO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring the operating system is configured for the current strategy.
When absent: execution machinery runs efficiently but in the wrong direction.

Aligns leadership behaviour, capability development, and organisational trust with the strategic direction. The CHRO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring the human system has the capacity, engagement, and psychological safety to carry the strategy forward.
When absent: strategy consistently exceeds the human system’s capacity to carry it.

Aligns technology architecture and data capability with strategic priorities and future operating model. The CTO/CIO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring technology investments actually change how the organisation works.
When absent: technology investments produce demonstrations with no capability shift.

Aligns market positioning and brand promise with the organisation’s operational ability to deliver. The CMO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring demand created externally can be fulfilled internally — and that the brand promise is one the organisation can keep consistently.
When absent: market signals are disconnected from strategic direction and brand promises outpace operational reality.

Aligns revenue generation and customer growth strategies with enterprise positioning and operational capacity. The CCO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring all revenue is strategic revenue — deals that strengthen distinctive positioning.
When absent: growth strategies create internal incoherence compounding over time.

Ensures procurement decisions strengthen operational capability and reinforce strategic priorities. The CPO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring cost efficiency decisions serve the customer’s end-game and the strategy’s priorities.
When absent: procurement optimises for cost at the expense of strategic capability.

Aligns enterprise risk interpretation so that strategic initiatives operate within a shared risk appetite framework. The CRO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring risk assessment enables strategic ambition.
When absent: risk appetite becomes function-by-function interpretation, creating asymmetric exposure.

Maintains the integrity of the strategic narrative as it moves from formulation into execution. The CSO’s alignment responsibility is ensuring strategy survives the transition from idea to implementation — that intent does not mutate as it moves through the organisation.
When absent: the strategic narrative fragments and different layers execute different versions of the strategy.
What is the most important alignment conversation you need to have with a closely adjacent role in the next 30 days? What would that conversation need to address?
prompts: ✎ Reflection What is the most important alignment conversation you need to have with a closely adjacent role in the next 30 days? What would that conversation need to address?
